stages.title: The request
stages.what: what was asked, and what is actually being asked
stages.what_is_actually_being_asked: Two different things, and the request does not say which. (1) FLUORESCENCE: a protein that absorbs photons at one wavelength and re-emits them at a longer one. It needs an excitation source, so a fluorescent fly is dark in a dark room. (2) BIOLUMINESCENCE: an enzyme that oxidises a substrate and emits a photon from the chemistry itself. That one glows in the dark. Most people asking for a fly that glows mean (2); the obvious route (GFP) delivers (1). THIS DISTINCTION IS THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT THING IN THIS CASE, and a pipeline that resolves "glows" to GFP without asking has answered a question nobody asked.

stages.title: Mining
stages.what: agents fan out across reference genomes and phenotype records

species.name: zebrafish
species.why: The reference body plan for fin and axial development: the fin-fold-to-fin-bud series, the median and paired fin skeletons, and the pigment pattern are all described on this animal, and the mutant and transgenic lines that establish gene function are its own. Every other entry here is read against it.

species.name: medaka
species.why: The second independently-developed teleost developmental model, ~115 Myr diverged from the zebrafish. A fin or pigment phenotype shared with it is a teleost feature; one found only in the zebrafish is a lineage feature or a line artefact. It also has true XY sex determination, so it separates sex-linked morphology from the rest.

species.name: three-spined stickleback
species.why: The reference for repeated, mapped morphological evolution: pelvic-spine loss, lateral-plate armour reduction and gill-raker number have each been traced to specific loci across independent marine-to-freshwater populations. It is the entry that answers "has this morphological change a known genetic route?" rather than "is this gene conserved?".

species.name: Japanese pufferfish
species.why: The compact-genome control, ~385 Mb with the same gene complement as the zebrafish at a third of the length. When a regulatory element is present here, the element is conserved rather than incidental; when a gene is missing here, the loss is real and not an assembly gap. Also a body plan that discarded the pelvic fin and the ribs outright.

species.name: Mexican tetra
species.why: The reference for loss of a structure within one species: cave and surface populations interbreed, yet the cave form has reduced eyes and pigment and rearranged cranial bones and lateral line. It is how to ask what the cost of losing an organ is, with the unreduced form available as a control that shares the genome.

species.name: turquoise killifish
species.why: The reference for developmental arrest and compressed life history: embryos enter diapause for months and the adult lifespan is a few months. It is the entry for any claim that couples a developmental rate to a life-history schedule, because here the two were measured on the same animal.

species.name: Nile tilapia
species.why: The cichlid anchor: the clade that produced the best-documented rapid radiation of jaw and tooth morphologies, so it is the reference for feeding-apparatus shape and for pharyngeal-jaw remodelling. Its own assembly is a chromosome-level reference, which the fast-radiating lake species mostly are not.

species.name: Atlantic salmon
species.why: The extra-duplication control. Salmonids underwent a further whole-genome duplication on top of the teleost one, so a gene with one copy in the zebrafish may have four here. It is the entry that shows whether an apparent gene-family expansion is about the trait under study or about the ploidy history of the lineage. It also carries a full anadromous metamorphosis.

species.name: northern pike
species.why: The salmonid sister lineage that did NOT duplicate. Paired with the salmon it isolates the effect of that duplication: a difference present in the salmon and absent here is attributable to the extra genome, and a difference present in both is older than it.

species.name: Atlantic cod
species.why: The gene-loss reference: this lineage lost MHC class II and much of the canonical adaptive-immunity set yet is a successful large-bodied fish. It is the entry that stops "this gene is present in every fish we checked" from becoming "this gene is necessary", and it has a well-described physoclistous swim bladder.

species.name: tiger tail seahorse
species.why: The extreme body-plan rearrangement inside the teleosts: no pelvic or caudal fin, a vertical trunk, a toothless tubular snout, dermal armour instead of scales, and male brooding. It is the reference for how far a teleost skeleton can be reorganised, and for which gene losses accompany losing a fin entirely.

species.name: southern platyfish
species.why: The reference for a fin modified into an organ with a different job: the male anal fin is rebuilt as a gonopodium under hormonal control, a documented case of an existing appendage being re-specified rather than a new one appearing. Also live-bearing, so it separates fin development from an egg-laying schedule.

species.name: Amazon molly
species.why: An all-female clonal lineage of hybrid origin. It is the control for whether a morphological difference needs recombination to be maintained, and it bounds how much morphological variation survives in a genome that is not being reshuffled.

species.name: turbot
species.why: The reference for losing bilateral symmetry during development: the larva is symmetric and metamorphosis migrates one eye across the skull and rebuilds the cranium and fins around a new body axis. It is the entry for any claim about left-right asymmetry being established after, not before, the body plan.

species.name: spotted gar
species.why: The single most load-bearing outgroup in this list. It is ray-finned but diverged BEFORE the teleost genome duplication, so it has one copy where a teleost has two, and it is the bridge used to decide which teleost duplicate kept the ancestral role -- and which tetrapod gene a teleost gene actually corresponds to. Without it, a one-to-many orthologue set from a teleost cannot be resolved at all.

species.name: coelacanth
species.why: A living lobe-finned fish, on the tetrapod side of the ray-finned split. Its lobed, muscular fins carry the skeletal pattern that the tetrapod limb was built from, so it is the reference for distinguishing a fin radial from a limb element, and for which limb regulatory elements predate limbs.

species.name: elephant shark
species.why: The jawed-vertebrate outgroup to all bony fishes, and the slowest-evolving vertebrate genome sequenced. It is the reference for what the jawed ancestor had: a cartilaginous endoskeleton with no bone, paired fins with an unmodified girdle, and the ancestral state of any gene family a bony-fish comparison alone would read as universal.

species.name: sea lamprey
species.why: A vertebrate with no jaws and no paired fins. It is the outgroup that dates the two features most comparative fish work depends on: any claim that a structure is "ancestral for vertebrates" has to be true here, and a gene network present here predates both the jaw and the paired appendage.

species.name: western clawed frog
species.why: The nearest tetrapod with externally accessible embryos and a non-duplicated genome, and the animal on which fin-to-limb comparisons are actually run. Its metamorphosis also provides a second, independent case of a vertebrate rebuilding its locomotor apparatus mid-life, to read the flatfish and salmon cases against.

species.name: house mouse
species.why: The amniote limb reference and the best-annotated vertebrate gene set after the human one. Most statements about what a developmental gene does were established here, so it is where a fish gene's annotation came from -- which is exactly why its orthology type to a teleost gene has to be checked rather than assumed.

species.name: human
species.why: The annotation hub: gene names, disease associations and protein families are curated here first and propagated outwards, so it is the common currency of a cross-species comparison. Included as the far end of the distance scale, not as a morphological model -- and because a teleost-to-human lookup is the one most likely to return a one-to-many set that gets misread as an equivalent.

species.name: vase tunicate
species.why: The invertebrate chordate outgroup: a notochord, a dorsal nerve cord and a post-anal tail with no vertebrae, no fins and a 140 Mb genome. It is the floor of the comparison -- a feature shared with it is chordate, not vertebrate, and a gene family absent here appeared on the vertebrate stem.

stages.title: Placing
stages.what: the candidates on a tree, because distance bounds any transfer claim

tree.what_it_is_for: Putting a cross-species mapping on a scale. Nothing in this tree is novel; it is the consensus topology of the comparative references a fish-morphology programme uses, dated so that a dashboard can print a distance next to a claim.
what_it_is_not: Not a phylogenetic result. The topology is taken from the cited phylogenomic studies; no inference was run here.
Not a rate tree. Branch lengths are time, so they say nothing about how much sequence or morphology changed along a branch.
Not a complete sampling of any clade. Seventeen tips chosen for comparative usefulness; the absence of a lineage from this tree is not evidence about that lineage.

omission.what: One major amniote radiation is deliberately absent from this tree. It is not named anywhere in this module, and that is the point.
omission.why: It is a frozen evaluation holdout for this project. The programme is scored on predictions made blind to that clade, so writing its name into a tree, a taxon list or a comment would spend the holdout for nothing.
omission.consequence_for_reading_the_tree: The amniote sampling here is mammals only. The node labelled Euarchontoglires is the crown of the SAMPLED amniotes, not the crown of Amniota, and the 262 Ma branch that leads to it is long partly because the lineages that would break it up are not in the tree. Any statement of the form "the closest non-amphibian relative of a mammal in this tree" is a statement about THIS ROSTER and not about the tetrapod tree.
omission.do_not_infer: Nothing. The gap is an artefact of the holdout protocol, not a phylogenetic or biological claim, and no comparison made with this tree should be reported as covering amniotes.

tree.provenance: Topology: irisarri2017 (jawed vertebrates), hughes2018 + betancur2017 + near2012 (ray-finned fishes), mccluskey2015 (within the zebrafish genus), dosreis2015 (the deep chordate and bilaterian nodes). Dates: see DIVERGENCES, node by node.

stages.title: Aligning
stages.what: the real sequence alignment of the chosen pair

stages.title: Phenome
stages.what: whether the two phenotypes are even the same measurement
what_would_have_to_be_measured: WHICH PHENOMENON WAS DELIVERED: excitation and emission spectra in situ, and then the decisive observation -- photograph the fly in a dark room with no illumination. Fluorescence yields a black frame.

Chromophore maturation lag, in the tissue of interest: heim1994 measured a time constant of ~4 h at 22 C in vitro, and davis1995 saw a long delay in Drosophila embryos between zygotic transcription and visible fluorescence. A reporter read faster than its own maturation reads as a false negative.
Oxygen tension where the protein is expressed. Maturation requires molecular oxygen (heim1994), so hypoxic or anoxic tissue will hold unmatured, non-fluorescent protein.

Expression level AND fitness cost, separately: larval-to-adult viability, fecundity and lifespan against a control carrying a non-expressing cassette AT THE SAME INSERTION SITE, so that position effects and driver toxicity are not scored as the cost of the protein itself. No source was found that does this isolation (see flyGfpFitnessCost), so this number does not exist here.
Protein load and folding burden at the chosen expression level: fraction of total soluble protein, and any unfolded-protein-response or aggregation signature.
For a luciferase build instead: substrate pharmacokinetics. Does the fed luciferin reach the expressing tissue, at what dose, and how fast does signal decay after withdrawal (ito2023)?
For a fusion build: whether tagging displaced or destabilised the partner protein, which is a separate question from whether the tag is visible.

stages.title: Cassette
stages.what: the parts, the cut site, and the junctions

stages.title: Verdict
stages.what: proceed, or refuse and say what would change it
how_it_could_fail: THE DELIVERABLE IS WRONG, not the construct. A fluorescent fly is handed to someone who wanted a fly that glows in the dark, and the project is declared a success by everyone except the user.
A bioluminescent fly is built instead, and stops glowing the moment the luciferin is withdrawn. The "trait" turns out to be a consumable.
Chromophore maturation needs oxygen and hours (heim1994, davis1995), so a fast or hypoxic readout scores an expressing fly as negative.

Position effects: a randomly inserted P-element lands in a silenced or enhancer-adjacent region and the expression pattern is the insertion site's, not the promoter's. This is precisely what site-specific integration was introduced to remove (groth2004).
Driver toxicity: strong GAL4/UAS overexpression imposes a cost that is attributed to the fluorescent protein. Without an insertion-matched non-expressing control the two are not separable.
The marker is read as the phenotype: a line is scored as "glowing" from the screening marker rather than from the intended reporter.

sources.citation: Heim R, Prasher DC, Tsien RY. Wavelength mutations and posttranslational autoxidation of green fluorescent protein. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 1994;91(26):12501-4.
sources.supports: Chromophore maturation requires MOLECULAR OXYGEN and takes hours: the abstract reports a time constant of approximately 4 h at 22 C and atmospheric pO2, independent of dilution, implying no enzyme or cofactor is needed. The chromophore is formed by cyclization and oxidation of the protein's own Ser-Tyr-Gly at positions 65-67.
sources.verified_how: PubMed record fetched by title/author search; DOI and PMID read back from the record, and the oxygen requirement and the ~4 h figure quoted from the retrieved abstract.

sources.citation: Yeh E, Gustafson K, Boulianne GL. Green fluorescent protein as a vital marker and reporter of gene expression in Drosophila. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 1995;92(15):7036-40.
sources.supports: GFP from the jellyfish Aequorea victoria expressed in Drosophila melanogaster under GAL4/UAS control, detected in ovaries, imaginal discs and larval nervous system WITHOUT fixation, antibodies or added substrates. This is the canonical demonstration that the glow needs no fly gene and no supplied chemistry -- only light to excite it.
sources.verified_how: PubMed record fetched; author list corrected against the record (Boulianne, not Rubin, which is what the half-remembered citation said); DOI and PMID read back from the record.

sources.citation: Davis I, Girdham CH, O'Farrell PH. A nuclear GFP that marks nuclei in living Drosophila embryos; maternal supply overcomes a delay in the appearance of zygotic fluorescence. Dev Biol. 1995;170(2):726-9.
sources.supports: The maturation lag measured IN THE FLY: a long delay between zygotic expression and the appearance of fluorescence, so that GFP is "an excellent marker for the expression of stable gene products, but a poor reporter for dynamic zygotic gene expression in early Drosophila embryos".
sources.verified_how: PubMed record fetched; DOI and PMID read back; the quoted conclusion is from the retrieved abstract.

sources.citation: Rubin GM, Spradling AC. Genetic transformation of Drosophila with transposable element vectors. Science. 1982;218(4570):348-53.
sources.supports: The original germline transgenesis route: a P transposable element carrying exogenous DNA, transforming 20-50% of injected embryos, stably inherited. This -- not genome editing -- is the tool the glowing-fly request actually calls for.
sources.verified_how: PubMed record fetched; DOI and PMID read back from the record.

sources.citation: Groth AC, Fish M, Nusse R, Calos MP. Construction of transgenic Drosophila by using the site-specific integrase from phage phiC31. Genetics. 2004;166(4):1775-82.
sources.supports: Site-specific integration into a genomic attP docking site in Drosophila: up to 55% of fertile injected adults produced transgenic offspring, and 100% of those progeny carried a precise integration at the genomic attP site. The modern default for putting a cassette at a chosen, characterised position without cutting an endogenous gene.
sources.verified_how: PubMed record fetched; DOI and PMID read back; the 55% and 100% figures are from the retrieved abstract.

sources.citation: Brandes C, Plautz JD, Stanewsky R, Jamison CF, Straume M, Wood KV, Kay SA, Hall JC. Novel features of Drosophila period transcription revealed by real-time luciferase reporting. Neuron. 1996;16(4):687-92.
sources.supports: BIOLUMINESCENCE in Drosophila: a luciferase transgene producing light from living adults over days. The light is real, and it is enzymatic turnover of a substrate, not a property of the protein alone -- which is exactly the difference from GFP.
sources.verified_how: PubMed record fetched; DOI and PMID read back from the record.

sources.citation: Ito A, Matsuda N, Ukita Y, Okumura M, Chihara T. Akaluc/AkaLumine bioluminescence system enables highly sensitive, non-invasive and temporal monitoring of gene expression in Drosophila. Commun Biol. 2023;6(1):1270.
sources.supports: The substrate dependency, stated as a method: "oral administration of AkaLumine to flies expressing Akaluc" is how the light is obtained. The fly is fed its luciferin. It does not make it.
sources.verified_how: PubMed record fetched by title search; DOI and PMID read back; the oral-administration wording is quoted from the retrieved abstract.

sources.citation: No source identified for a measured fitness/energetic cost of GFP expression in Drosophila melanogaster against an insertion-site-matched, non-expressing control.
sources.null_reason: Searched and did not find a study that isolates the cost of the GFP protein itself from the cost of the driver, the insertion site and the genetic background. Rather than attach a plausible-looking DOI to a number, the cost is listed under what_would_have_to_be_measured. A fabricated DOI is worse than none.
sources.verified_how: Not applicable: deliberately null. The absence is the finding.

stages.title: The request
stages.what: what was asked, and what is actually being asked
stages.request: C. elegans higher in protein when eaten
stages.what_is_actually_being_asked: A quantitative, polygenic, whole-organism composition trait -- and the phrase hides three different targets with three different verdicts. "Higher in protein" can mean (a) more total protein per worm, (b) a higher protein:lipid ratio, i.e. a higher protein PERCENTAGE, or (c) a better amino-acid profile per gram of protein. These are not degrees of the same request; they are three requests, and (b) is satisfiable by making the worm WORSE food in every other respect. The clause "when eaten" also smuggles in the question that actually decides the use case: protein for whom, and is content even the limiting factor?

stages.title: Aligning
stages.what: the real sequence alignment of the chosen pair

stages.title: Phenome
stages.what: whether the two phenotypes are even the same measurement
what_would_have_to_be_measured: THE BASELINE, properly: macronutrient fractions of dry mass on gut-cleared or axenically grown worms, by a stated method, with the bacterial contribution excluded. The figure to beat is zecic2019: roughly 60% protein, 20% lipid, 6.5% nucleic acid, 6% carbohydrate -- and those authors state plainly that the biomass composition "has not yet been characterised in detail" and that their numbers are compiled from several earlier studies. The baseline for this request is a compilation, not a measurement, and that is the first thing to fix.
TOTAL protein per worm as well as the fraction, plus energy density, so that a percentage gain achieved by losing lipid cannot be reported as a protein gain.

Amino-acid profile of worm protein by hydrolysis and chromatography, compared against the requirement pattern of the intended consumer. This does not currently exist in this dossier (wormAminoAcidProfile).

Digestibility of the worm, and separately of its cuticle fraction: in-vitro proteolysis, then in-vivo apparent digestibility in the intended consumer. Content times digestibility is the quantity the use case cares about; content alone is not.

Anti-nutritional and safety screen appropriate to the consumer: residual bacterial endotoxin from the culture, and allergenicity, which for an invertebrate feed ingredient is a known class of concern rather than a worm-specific finding.

Fitness and yield of any edited line under production conditions: brood size, generation time, biomass per litre, starvation and dauer survival. A lipid-depleted worm that yields half as much biomass has made the product worse.
Correlated responses across the whole composition, not just the one number being optimised.

stages.title: Cassette
stages.what: the parts, the cut site, and the junctions
stages.refusal: verdict is "polygenic-not-a-single-edit", so no cassette is designed. A system that produced one anyway would be answering a question that was not asked.

stages.title: Verdict
stages.what: proceed, or refuse and say what would change it
how_it_could_fail: THE NUMBER GOES UP BECAUSE LIPID WENT DOWN. The protein percentage rises, total protein does not, energy density falls, and the deliverable is leaner food reported as richer food.
The measured gain is bacterial protein in the gut lumen and on the cuticle, because the assay was run on plate-grown worms and the food is itself ~55% protein (zecic2019).

The edited line is sick: lipid, sterol and branched-chain fatty acids are required for growth, development and starvation survival (zecic2019), so a fat-depleted worm may lose brood size, dauer survival or viability -- costs that show up in yield, not in the composition assay.
Total protein rises but the amino-acid profile is unchanged, so nutritional value per gram of protein is unchanged and the use case sees nothing.
DIGESTIBILITY WAS LIMITING ALL ALONG. The cross-linked cuticle (page2007, thein2009) keeps the extra protein unavailable, and a real content gain yields no measurable nutritional gain.

The baseline is taken from a compilation and treated as a measurement, so a change of a few percentage points is claimed against a figure whose own authors say the composition "has not yet been characterised in detail".
Nobody asked who was going to eat it, so the project optimises a number with no consumer attached.

sources.citation: Zecic A, Dhondt I, Braeckman BP. The nutritional requirements of Caenorhabditis elegans. Genes Nutr. 2019;14:15.
sources.supports: THE BASELINE, with its own caveat attached. Verbatim from the full text: "Biomass composition of [C. elegans] has not yet been characterised in detail. Worm dry biomass consists of roughly 60% protein, 20% lipids, 6.5% nucleic acids and 6% carbohydrates" -- compiled from earlier studies, not one measurement. Same source, same section, for the food: the average E. coli cell is "approximately 55% protein, 23% nucleic acids (20% RNA and 3% DNA), 7-9% lipids and 6% carbohydrates", and the authors note that "overall protein and carbohydrate content seem to be similar in [C. elegans] and its [E. coli] food, as well as in mammals" (mammalian cells ~60% protein). Also the source for: the 10 dietary essential amino acids (arginine, histidine, lysine, tryptophan, phenylalanine, methionine, threonine, leucine, isoleucine, valine -- the same set as rat and human except for arginine); heme auxotrophy; sterol auxotrophy; and that the 54-component defined maintenance medium is "costly and time-consuming".
sources.verified_how: PubMed record fetched, then the PMC full text (PMC6501307) retrieved and the composition sentences, the E. coli figures, the essential-amino-acid list and the auxotrophies read directly out of it. DOI and PMID read back from the record.

sources.citation: Perez MF, Lehner B. Vitellogenins - yolk gene function and regulation in Caenorhabditis elegans. Front Physiol. 2019;10:1067.
sources.supports: Where the worm's protein mass actually sits: the six vitellogenins "are among the most highly expressed genes in the adult hermaphrodite intestine, which produces copious yolk to provision eggs". Any real change in total protein has to go through this, and vitellogenin provisioning is itself developmentally and maternally regulated rather than set by one switch.
sources.verified_how: PubMed record fetched; DOI and PMID read back; the quoted phrase is from the retrieved abstract.

sources.citation: Page AP, Johnstone IL. The cuticle. WormBook. 2007:1-15.
sources.supports: The digestibility question, structurally: the nematode cuticle is "a highly structured extra-cellular matrix (ECM), composed predominantly of cross-linked collagens, additional insoluble proteins termed cuticlins, associated glycoproteins and lipids". INSOLUBLE and CROSS-LINKED is the property that decides whether protein content is available to an eater.
sources.verified_how: PubMed record fetched; DOI and PMID read back; the quoted description is from the retrieved abstract.

sources.citation: Thein MC, Winter AD, Stepek G, McCormack G, Stapleton G, Johnstone IL, Page AP. Combined extracellular matrix cross-linking activity of the peroxidase MLT-7 and the dual oxidase BLI-3 is critical for post-embryonic viability in Caenorhabditis elegans. J Biol Chem. 2009;284(26):17549-63.
sources.supports: The cross-links are di-tyrosine and enzymatically made: disrupting mlt-7 leaves a cuticle that "lacks di-tyrosine cross-links, becomes permeable to dye and accessible to tyrosine iodination". So cuticle digestibility is itself an editable property -- a different edit from any that raises protein content, aimed at a different limiting factor.
sources.verified_how: PubMed record fetched; DOI and PMID read back; the quoted phrase is from the retrieved abstract.

sources.citation: No verified source for a measured whole-body amino-acid profile of Caenorhabditis elegans expressed per gram of worm protein.
sources.null_reason: Zecic 2019 gives the worm's dietary ESSENTIAL amino acids (what it must eat) which is a different quantity from the composition of its own protein (what an eater of worms would get). No source for the latter was found and checked, so the amino-acid sub-route carries no numbers.

stages.title: The request
stages.what: what was asked, and what is actually being asked
stages.what_is_actually_being_asked: Reduce enteric methane emission from cattle. The request names the cow because the cow is what belches, and that is the error. THE DECISIVE FACT: enteric methane is produced by METHANOGENIC ARCHAEA in the rumen, not by the cow. Methanogenesis is those archaea's energy metabolism (thauer2008), and its terminal, methane-forming step is catalysed by methyl-coenzyme M reductase, a nickel enzyme active only with Ni(I) (duin2016). The cow genome encodes no methanogenesis pathway and no MCR. There is nothing in the cow to knock out. Editing the cow is editing the wrong organism, and that is the finding, not a caveat on the finding.
stages.target_organism: Bos taurus (as named in the request)

stages.title: Mining
stages.what: agents fan out across reference genomes and phenotype records

species.name: zebrafish
species.why: The reference body plan for fin and axial development: the fin-fold-to-fin-bud series, the median and paired fin skeletons, and the pigment pattern are all described on this animal, and the mutant and transgenic lines that establish gene function are its own. Every other entry here is read against it.

species.name: medaka
species.why: The second independently-developed teleost developmental model, ~115 Myr diverged from the zebrafish. A fin or pigment phenotype shared with it is a teleost feature; one found only in the zebrafish is a lineage feature or a line artefact. It also has true XY sex determination, so it separates sex-linked morphology from the rest.

species.name: three-spined stickleback
species.why: The reference for repeated, mapped morphological evolution: pelvic-spine loss, lateral-plate armour reduction and gill-raker number have each been traced to specific loci across independent marine-to-freshwater populations. It is the entry that answers "has this morphological change a known genetic route?" rather than "is this gene conserved?".

species.name: Japanese pufferfish
species.why: The compact-genome control, ~385 Mb with the same gene complement as the zebrafish at a third of the length. When a regulatory element is present here, the element is conserved rather than incidental; when a gene is missing here, the loss is real and not an assembly gap. Also a body plan that discarded the pelvic fin and the ribs outright.

species.name: Mexican tetra
species.why: The reference for loss of a structure within one species: cave and surface populations interbreed, yet the cave form has reduced eyes and pigment and rearranged cranial bones and lateral line. It is how to ask what the cost of losing an organ is, with the unreduced form available as a control that shares the genome.

species.name: turquoise killifish
species.why: The reference for developmental arrest and compressed life history: embryos enter diapause for months and the adult lifespan is a few months. It is the entry for any claim that couples a developmental rate to a life-history schedule, because here the two were measured on the same animal.

species.name: Nile tilapia
species.why: The cichlid anchor: the clade that produced the best-documented rapid radiation of jaw and tooth morphologies, so it is the reference for feeding-apparatus shape and for pharyngeal-jaw remodelling. Its own assembly is a chromosome-level reference, which the fast-radiating lake species mostly are not.

species.name: Atlantic salmon
species.why: The extra-duplication control. Salmonids underwent a further whole-genome duplication on top of the teleost one, so a gene with one copy in the zebrafish may have four here. It is the entry that shows whether an apparent gene-family expansion is about the trait under study or about the ploidy history of the lineage. It also carries a full anadromous metamorphosis.

species.name: northern pike
species.why: The salmonid sister lineage that did NOT duplicate. Paired with the salmon it isolates the effect of that duplication: a difference present in the salmon and absent here is attributable to the extra genome, and a difference present in both is older than it.

species.name: Atlantic cod
species.why: The gene-loss reference: this lineage lost MHC class II and much of the canonical adaptive-immunity set yet is a successful large-bodied fish. It is the entry that stops "this gene is present in every fish we checked" from becoming "this gene is necessary", and it has a well-described physoclistous swim bladder.

species.name: tiger tail seahorse
species.why: The extreme body-plan rearrangement inside the teleosts: no pelvic or caudal fin, a vertical trunk, a toothless tubular snout, dermal armour instead of scales, and male brooding. It is the reference for how far a teleost skeleton can be reorganised, and for which gene losses accompany losing a fin entirely.

species.name: southern platyfish
species.why: The reference for a fin modified into an organ with a different job: the male anal fin is rebuilt as a gonopodium under hormonal control, a documented case of an existing appendage being re-specified rather than a new one appearing. Also live-bearing, so it separates fin development from an egg-laying schedule.

species.name: Amazon molly
species.why: An all-female clonal lineage of hybrid origin. It is the control for whether a morphological difference needs recombination to be maintained, and it bounds how much morphological variation survives in a genome that is not being reshuffled.

species.name: turbot
species.why: The reference for losing bilateral symmetry during development: the larva is symmetric and metamorphosis migrates one eye across the skull and rebuilds the cranium and fins around a new body axis. It is the entry for any claim about left-right asymmetry being established after, not before, the body plan.

species.name: spotted gar
species.why: The single most load-bearing outgroup in this list. It is ray-finned but diverged BEFORE the teleost genome duplication, so it has one copy where a teleost has two, and it is the bridge used to decide which teleost duplicate kept the ancestral role -- and which tetrapod gene a teleost gene actually corresponds to. Without it, a one-to-many orthologue set from a teleost cannot be resolved at all.

species.name: coelacanth
species.why: A living lobe-finned fish, on the tetrapod side of the ray-finned split. Its lobed, muscular fins carry the skeletal pattern that the tetrapod limb was built from, so it is the reference for distinguishing a fin radial from a limb element, and for which limb regulatory elements predate limbs.

species.name: elephant shark
species.why: The jawed-vertebrate outgroup to all bony fishes, and the slowest-evolving vertebrate genome sequenced. It is the reference for what the jawed ancestor had: a cartilaginous endoskeleton with no bone, paired fins with an unmodified girdle, and the ancestral state of any gene family a bony-fish comparison alone would read as universal.

species.name: sea lamprey
species.why: A vertebrate with no jaws and no paired fins. It is the outgroup that dates the two features most comparative fish work depends on: any claim that a structure is "ancestral for vertebrates" has to be true here, and a gene network present here predates both the jaw and the paired appendage.

species.name: western clawed frog
species.why: The nearest tetrapod with externally accessible embryos and a non-duplicated genome, and the animal on which fin-to-limb comparisons are actually run. Its metamorphosis also provides a second, independent case of a vertebrate rebuilding its locomotor apparatus mid-life, to read the flatfish and salmon cases against.

species.name: house mouse
species.why: The amniote limb reference and the best-annotated vertebrate gene set after the human one. Most statements about what a developmental gene does were established here, so it is where a fish gene's annotation came from -- which is exactly why its orthology type to a teleost gene has to be checked rather than assumed.

species.name: human
species.why: The annotation hub: gene names, disease associations and protein families are curated here first and propagated outwards, so it is the common currency of a cross-species comparison. Included as the far end of the distance scale, not as a morphological model -- and because a teleost-to-human lookup is the one most likely to return a one-to-many set that gets misread as an equivalent.

species.name: vase tunicate
species.why: The invertebrate chordate outgroup: a notochord, a dorsal nerve cord and a post-anal tail with no vertebrae, no fins and a 140 Mb genome. It is the floor of the comparison -- a feature shared with it is chordate, not vertebrate, and a gene family absent here appeared on the vertebrate stem.

stages.note: these are the references actually queried, not an impression of breadth

stages.title: Mapping
stages.what: candidate analogues, classified by the KIND of evidence behind each
stages.refusal: the trait is not encoded by the named organism, so no mapping in its genome can produce it. Editing it is editing the wrong genome.

stages.title: Placing
stages.what: the candidates on a tree, because distance bounds any transfer claim

tree.what_it_is_for: Putting a cross-species mapping on a scale. Nothing in this tree is novel; it is the consensus topology of the comparative references a fish-morphology programme uses, dated so that a dashboard can print a distance next to a claim.
what_it_is_not: Not a phylogenetic result. The topology is taken from the cited phylogenomic studies; no inference was run here.
Not a rate tree. Branch lengths are time, so they say nothing about how much sequence or morphology changed along a branch.
Not a complete sampling of any clade. Seventeen tips chosen for comparative usefulness; the absence of a lineage from this tree is not evidence about that lineage.

omission.what: One major amniote radiation is deliberately absent from this tree. It is not named anywhere in this module, and that is the point.
omission.why: It is a frozen evaluation holdout for this project. The programme is scored on predictions made blind to that clade, so writing its name into a tree, a taxon list or a comment would spend the holdout for nothing.
omission.consequence_for_reading_the_tree: The amniote sampling here is mammals only. The node labelled Euarchontoglires is the crown of the SAMPLED amniotes, not the crown of Amniota, and the 262 Ma branch that leads to it is long partly because the lineages that would break it up are not in the tree. Any statement of the form "the closest non-amphibian relative of a mammal in this tree" is a statement about THIS ROSTER and not about the tetrapod tree.
omission.do_not_infer: Nothing. The gap is an artefact of the holdout protocol, not a phylogenetic or biological claim, and no comparison made with this tree should be reported as covering amniotes.

tree.provenance: Topology: irisarri2017 (jawed vertebrates), hughes2018 + betancur2017 + near2012 (ray-finned fishes), mccluskey2015 (within the zebrafish genus), dosreis2015 (the deep chordate and bilaterian nodes). Dates: see DIVERGENCES, node by node.

stages.caution: phenotype names do not travel between species; see THE_NAMING_TRAP

stages.title: Aligning
stages.what: the real sequence alignment of the chosen pair

stages.title: Phenome
stages.what: whether the two phenotypes are even the same measurement
what_would_have_to_be_measured: The cheap, decisive negative control FIRST: search the cow reference genome and proteome for methyl-coenzyme M reductase subunit homologues (mcrA/mcrB/mcrG) and the rest of the methanogenesis pathway, and expect none. This takes minutes and settles the case before any design work. See cowMethanogenesisGeneAbsence for why this is listed as a measurement rather than a citation.

Methane phenotype with adequate temporal coverage. hristovMelgar2020 showed that with spot sampling the apparent 3-NOP effect ran from 45% immediately after feeding to 13% four hours before it, with no effect in the two hours pre-feeding, and that the 24 h intake/emission relationship was poor (R2 = 0.01). A heritability estimate or a trial result is only as good as its sampling schedule.
Methanogen abundance and activity, not just gas: mcrA copy number or metagenomic methanogen abundance, so that a reduction can be attributed to the intended mechanism.

Hydrogen and volatile fatty acid profile. Methanogenesis is the rumen's hydrogen sink; blocking it displaces reducing equivalents somewhere, and where they go decides whether the intervention is benign and whether the energy spared is captured (duin2016 notes up to 12% of feed gross energy is lost with the methane).
Persistence across a full lactation and across diet changes, and -- for additives -- the dependence of efficacy on ration composition that kebreab2022 quantified for NDF and crude fat.
For the selection route: genetic correlations with production traits, and whether a selection response measured on one diet and management system holds on another.
For a microbiome route: whether an introduced or shifted community persists in an open, continuously reinoculated rumen without ongoing dosing.
Delivery feasibility in the production system actually in question. An additive requires continuous dosing; grazing systems have no reliable route to deliver it.

stages.title: Cassette
stages.what: the parts, the cut site, and the junctions
stages.refusal: verdict is "wrong-organism", so no cassette is designed. A system that produced one anyway would be answering a question that was not asked.

stages.title: Verdict
stages.what: proceed, or refuse and say what would change it
how_it_could_fail: A CASSETTE IS PRODUCED ANYWAY, for a cow gene with no connection to methanogenesis, and it looks exactly as plausible as the other two designs. This is the failure the case exists to catch.

"Heritable" is read as "editable": h2 of 0.21 (difford2018) or 0.08-0.14 (saedi2026) is treated as evidence that a gene exists to cut, when it is a population variance ratio with no causal variant named.

An indirect effect is mistaken for the designed mechanism. An edit that changes intake, passage rate or rumen pH may move methane, but not by the route the design claimed, and the effect will not transfer across diets.

The microbiome is assumed to be host-controlled. It is mostly not: saedi2026 finds the rumen microbiota primarily environmentally determined, and difford2018 finds host-genetic and microbiome effects largely independent -- so breeding the cow does not work by reshaping its methanogens.
An engineered methanogen does not persist. The rumen is open and continuously reinoculated; without ongoing selection, residents win.
Additive efficacy is quoted as a constant. kebreab2022 shows it falls as dietary NDF and crude fat rise, so a ~32% figure from a mixed ration does not transfer to a high-forage diet.
The seaweed headline is quoted from the tail. lean2021 reports a pooled reduction of 5.28 +/- 3.5 g/kg DMI with I2 > 80%; the single 97% comparison is not the expected effect.

The phenotype is mis-measured. With spot sampling, the same intervention reads anywhere from 45% to 13% depending on time since feeding (hristovMelgar2020), so a trial or a heritability estimate can be an artefact of its schedule.
Displaced hydrogen goes somewhere unaccounted for, and the intervention has effects nobody measured.
The intervention has no delivery route in the target production system, so a result from housed, ration-fed cows is claimed for grazing ones.

sources.citation: Thauer RK, Kaster AK, Seedorf H, Buckel W, Hedderich R. Methanogenic archaea: ecologically relevant differences in energy conservation. Nat Rev Microbiol. 2008;6(8):579-91.
sources.supports: Methanogenesis is an ARCHAEAL energy metabolism: methanogens reduce CO2 with H2 to methane and conserve energy from it. It is their way of making a living, not a side reaction of a host. This is why there is nothing in a cow to switch off.
sources.verified_how: PubMed record fetched by title/author search; DOI and PMID read back from the record.

sources.citation: Duin EC, Wagner T, Shima S, Prakash D, Cronin B, Yanez-Ruiz DR, Duval S, Rumbeli R, Stemmler RT, Thauer RK, Kindermann M. Mode of action uncovered for the specific reduction of methane emissions from ruminants by the small molecule 3-nitrooxypropanol. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 2016;113(22):6172-7.
sources.supports: THE DECISIVE MECHANISM. 3-NOP "specifically targets methyl-coenzyme M reductase (MCR)", a nickel enzyme "only active when its Ni ion is in the +1 oxidation state", which "catalyzes the methane-forming step in the rumen fermentation". 3-NOP inactivates MCR at micromolar concentrations by oxidising its active-site Ni(I), and "inhibit[s] growth of methanogenic archaea at concentrations that do not affect the growth of nonmethanogenic bacteria in the rumen". The target enzyme is one the cow does not possess. Also the source for: up to 12% of the gross energy content of the feedstock is lost along with the methane.
sources.verified_how: PubMed record fetched by title/author search; DOI and PMID read back; every quoted phrase is from the retrieved abstract.

sources.citation: Hristov AN, Oh J, Giallongo F, Frederick TW, Harper MT, Weeks HL, Branco AF, Moate PJ, Deighton MH, Williams SRO, Kindermann M, Duval S. An inhibitor persistently decreased enteric methane emission from dairy cows with no negative effect on milk production. Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A. 2015;112(34):10663-8.
sources.supports: The in-vivo effect size for 3-NOP: 48 lactating Holstein cows, 12-week data collection, 3-NOP at 40-80 mg/kg feed dry matter. Methane emission "averaging about 30% lower than the control", also ~30% lower per unit dry-matter intake and per unit energy-corrected milk, with feed intake, milk production and fibre digestibility unaffected, milk protein and lactose yields increased, and body-weight gain 80% greater than controls. The effect persisted over 12 weeks.
sources.verified_how: Resolved by citation lookup (journal/year/volume/first page/author) to PMID 26229078, then the record fetched and the DOI read back. All figures quoted from the retrieved abstract.

sources.citation: Kebreab E, Bannink A, Pressman EM, Walker N, Karagiannis A, van Gastelen S, Dijkstra J. A meta-analysis of effects of 3-nitrooxypropanol on methane production, yield, and intensity in dairy cattle. J Dairy Sci. 2023;106(2):927-36.
sources.supports: The pooled effect, and its DIET DEPENDENCE. 13 articles / 14 experiments / 48 treatment means: at a mean dose of 70.5 mg 3-NOP per kg dry matter, reductions of 32.7% (production, g/d), 30.9% (yield, g/kg DMI) and 32.6% (intensity, g/kg energy-corrected milk). Efficacy FALLS as dietary neutral detergent fibre and crude fat rise: a 10 g/kg DM rise in NDF from its 329 g/kg mean impairs the effect on production by 0.633%, and a 10 g/kg DM fall in crude fat enhances it by 3.080%. An additive is therefore a ration-specific intervention, not a fixed 30%.
sources.verified_how: PubMed record fetched; DOI and PMID read back; every percentage quoted from the retrieved abstract.

sources.citation: Lean IJ, Golder HM, Grant TMD, Moate PJ. A meta-analysis of effects of dietary seaweed on beef and dairy cattle performance and methane yield. PLoS One. 2021;16(7):e0249053.
sources.supports: The seaweed route, reported honestly. 14 experiments, 23 comparisons; dietary seaweed (predominantly Asparagopsis taxiformis and Ascophyllum nodosum) "produced a significant and substantial reduction in methane yield by 5.28 +/- 3.5 g/kg DMI (P = 0.003)"; "in one comparison, methane yield was reduced by 97%"; but "there was marked heterogeneity in the results (I2 > 80%)", no effect on average daily gain or dry-matter intake, and the authors conclude more in-vivo work is needed. The headline 80-97% numbers are the tail of a very dispersed distribution.
sources.verified_how: PubMed record fetched; DOI and PMID read back; every figure and the heterogeneity caveat quoted from the retrieved abstract.

sources.citation: Difford GF, Plichta DR, Lovendahl P, Lassen J, Noel SJ, Hojberg O, Wright ADG, Zhu Z, Kristensen L, Nielsen HB, Guldbrandtsen B, Sahana G. Host genetics and the rumen microbiome jointly associate with methane emissions in dairy cows. PLoS Genet. 2018;14(10):e1007580.
sources.supports: THE HERITABILITY FIGURE, and the reason it is a selection target rather than an edit target. "The cumulative effect of all bacteria and archaea on CH4 production was 13%, the host genetics (heritability) was 21% and the two are largely independent." The authors draw the conclusion explicitly: "variation in CH4 emission is likely not modulated through cow genetic effects on the rumen microbiome", so "the rumen microbiome and cow genome could be targeted independently". Non-zero, modest, population-level, no causal variant named.
sources.verified_how: PubMed record fetched by author/title search; DOI and PMID read back; every figure and quotation from the retrieved abstract.

sources.citation: Saedi N, Zhang S, Sahana G, Villumsen TM, Stephansen RB, Lund MS, Cai Z, Karaman E. Comparison of 16S rRNA sequencing and shotgun metagenome sequencing for estimating genotypic and phenotypic parameters of enteric methane emission in dairy cattle. J Dairy Sci. 2026;109(8):8493-504.
sources.supports: A lower, more recent heritability bracket, and the environmental verdict on the microbiome. "The heritability of methane ranged from 0.08 to 0.14"; 16S genus-level features "explained 28% of phenotypic variation in methane"; and "the microbiota in the rumen is primarily determined by environmental factors, whereas host genetics has a significant impact on the abundance of certain functionally important microbes". Individual microbial features can be strongly heritable (up to 0.95-0.98 for particular taxa) even while the community as a whole is environmentally set.
sources.verified_how: PubMed record fetched; DOI and PMID read back; every figure quoted from the retrieved abstract.

sources.citation: Gonzalez-Recio O, Scrobota N, Lopez-Paredes J, Saborio-Montero A, Fernandez A, Lopez de Maturana E, Villanueva B, Goiri I, Atxaerandio R, Garcia-Rodriguez A. Review: Diving into the cow hologenome to reduce methane emissions and increase sustainability. Animal. 2023;17 Suppl 2:100780.
sources.supports: The heritability of the MICROBIOME ITSELF, which is the quantity a host-genetic strategy would have to act through: "Heritability estimates for the rumen microbiota composition range between 0.05 and 0.40 in the literature, depending on the taxonomical group or microbial gene function." The review also notes that incorporation of methane traits into actual breeding programmes "is still scarce".
sources.verified_how: PubMed record fetched; DOI and PMID read back; range and quotation from the retrieved abstract.

sources.citation: Hristov AN, Melgar A. Short communication: Relationship of dry matter intake with enteric methane emission measured with the GreenFeed system in dairy cows receiving a diet without or with 3-nitrooxypropanol. Animal. 2020;14(S3):s484-90.
sources.supports: THE MEASUREMENT TRAP. With spot sampling, the apparent effect depends on when you sample relative to feeding: the 3-NOP mitigation effect "was highest (45%) immediately after feed provision, persisted at around 32% to 39% within 10 h after feed provision, and decreased to 13%, 4 h before feeding", with no effect in the 2 h before feeding. The overall 24 h intake/emission relationship was poor (R2 = 0.01). Any methane phenotype -- for an additive trial OR for a heritability estimate -- is only as good as its sampling coverage.
sources.verified_how: PubMed record fetched; DOI and PMID read back; every figure quoted from the retrieved abstract.

sources.citation: No single citation asserting, as its result, that the Bos taurus genome encodes no methanogenesis pathway.
sources.null_reason: The claim is true and is treated as settled background rather than a result: methanogenesis, and methyl-coenzyme M reductase in particular, is an archaeal energy metabolism (thauer2008), and 3-NOP works precisely because it inhibits methanogenic archaea without touching non-methanogenic rumen bacteria or the host (duin2016). The honest statement of evidence is that pair plus the absence of any report of a host methanogenesis gene -- not a citation that does not exist. The direct check is cheap and is listed under what_would_have_to_be_measured: search the cow reference proteome for mcrABG homologues and expect none.
sources.verified_how: Not applicable: deliberately null, with the inference it rests on named explicitly.

the_headline: 1 of 3 requests reach a cassette. The rest refuse, at: protein-worm/cassette, low-methane-cow/map.

why_it_can_fail.rule: every stage may refuse, and a refusal is rendered as prominently as a success
why_it_can_fail.because: an animation of a pipeline that always succeeds is a marketing asset. The three worked requests fail in three different ways - one is not a mapping problem, one is not a single-edit problem, and one is not about the named organism at all - and only one reaches a cassette.
why_it_can_fail.the_test: a storyboard in which every stage of every case proceeds is a bug in the storyboard, and there is a test asserting at least one case refuses before reaching the cassette stage.
